messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Caleb was thirty-seven when the quiet hum of his home server rack gave way to the violent clatter of an ambulance bay, marking the sudden onset of a life-threatening cardiac event. He remembered the crushing weight on his chest, the frantic paramedics pressing needles into his veins, and the terrifying sensation of the breathing tube forcing its way down his throat while monitors screamed in a relentless chorus. He survived the ICU stay, but the physical scars were merely the perimeter; the real damage settled into his cognitive landscape. Within weeks of discharge, his body refused to settle. His chest perpetually tightened, his muscles coiled as if bracing for another collapse, and any minor reminder of the hospital sent his heart hammering against his ribs. He found himself consumed by a sharp, unrelenting anger at his own fragility and a heavy shame over leaving his daughter alone during the darkest hours. His body remained wired, reacting violently to labored respiration, the sight of a tourniquet, or the glint of medical tubing, turning every ordinary moment into a potential relapse. Because his nervous system stayed locked in a state of high alert and his mind flooded with fear and guilt, Caleb systematically dismantled his daily routine to regain a sense of safety. He stopped going to the gym, convinced that any elevated heart rate would restart the crisis. He began tracking calories with obsessive precision, cutting his portions until eating felt like managing a dangerous system, the only variable he could control when his body felt like a liability. He also established a strict rule never to step inside urgent care facilities or answer emergency hold calls, routing his database administration work exclusively through a remote terminal to keep himself isolated from any scene that might require an ambulance or a physical examination. Over the following months, this rigid isolation only sharpened his sensitivity to the very things he fled. His complete avoidance of physical exertion meant that even walking to his home server rack left him suddenly winded, and that abrupt breathlessness instantly pulled him back to the ventilator tubes that had first stolen his air. Every time he glanced at his coffee maker’s tubing or a contractor’s glucose monitor during a remote audit, the needle imagery flared, unbuffered by any real intervention. Worse, his strict dietary restriction and total physical inactivity left his nervous system utterly unconditioned to stress; the moment a minor cough echoed in his shared office breakroom, his shoulders locked and a fresh wave of dread crashed over him, proving that the safety behaviors he relied on were only feeding the alarm rather than silencing it. By the time he scheduled his intake, the quiet architecture of his professional life had frayed. The constant vigilance and caloric counting drained his focus, and the avoidance of medical settings left a nagging, unaddressed phantom pain in his ribs. What finally drove him to the clinic was a Tuesday afternoon when a simple blood draw at a routine occupational screening sent him into full panic, forcing him to abandon his workstation and call in sick for the third time that month. Sitting in the waiting room now, Caleb fears he is slowly hollowing himself out through precautions that only deepen his vulnerability, hoping instead that a clinician might help him untangle the wires before his own safety behaviors become his cage.
